summaries.Q269273: Founded in 1565, it is the oldest riding school still in existence in the world. It trains only Lipizzaner stallions and gives its performances in the Winter Riding School, built between 1729 and 1735 near the Hofburg. By tradition the riders salute the portrait of Emperor Charles VI before beginning their figures.
summaries.Q1317970: A white arch decorated with muses shelters at its centre the gilded bronze statue of the composer Johann Strauss II playing the violin; the base is marble. The design by Alfred Castelliz and Edmund von Hellmer won the 1906 competition, but the First World War delayed the work: the unveiling took place on 26 June 1921.
summaries.Q478455: A museum of decorative arts and design, it also gives an important place to contemporary art. The Stubenring building, designed by Heinrich von Ferstel, was erected in 1871; since 2004 James Turrell's permanent outdoor installation MAKlite has lit it up in the evening. The collections exceed 300,000 objects.
summaries.Q638493: The museum occupies the former Thonet furniture factory, an 1892 building renovated from 1989 to 1991 to plans by Friedensreich Hundertwasser, in his own style: undulating floors, bright colours, chequerboard mosaics, few straight lines. It holds the world's only permanent exhibition of the artist's works.
summaries.Q874557: The philosopher Ludwig Wittgenstein drew the plans for this house and built it in 1927-1928 with Jacques Groag and Paul Engelmann, both pupils of Adolf Loos, at the request of his sister Margarethe Stonborough. The building is modernist, inspired by Loos's anti-ornamentalism. In 2018 it housed the Bulgarian Cultural Institute.
summaries.Q264752: A vast green expanse between the Danube and the Danube Canal, the Prater is mentioned as early as 1403, then enclosed in 1560 by Maximilian II as a Habsburg hunting reserve; Joseph II opened it to the public in 1766. It holds a permanent funfair, the Ernst Happel Stadium and the Wiener Riesenrad, built in 1897 and nearly 65 m high.
summaries.Q693884: A fire destroyed almost all of the earlier church in 1661. The present Baroque building was erected on the initiative of Leopold I, to plans by Gabriele Montani modified in 1703 by Johann Lucas von Hildebrandt. It is the first church in Vienna with a Baroque dome, and its nave is oval. Priests of Opus Dei serve it.
summaries.Q279260: Founded in 1876 by restaurateur Eduard Sacher on the site of the former Theater am Kärntnertor, this hotel was at first only a furnished house, the Hotel de l'Opera. Anna Sacher, who inherited it on her husband's death, made it one of the world's most refined hotels. Its speciality is the Sachertorte, invented by Eduard's father Franz Sacher.
summaries.Q695126: Built between 1911 and 1913 to plans by Ferdinand Fellner and Hermann Helmer, with the collaboration of Ludwig Baumann, the Konzerthaus was inaugurated on 19 October 1913 by Richard Strauss. Fully renovated between 1997 and 2000, it houses four halls, from the Great Hall with 1,840 seats to the Schubert Hall with 336.
summaries.Q390730: Home to the Jewish community since the 12th century, the square was called Schulhof until the pogrom of 1420-1421. An edict of Frederick II authorised various buildings there in 1238, among them a synagogue. It holds a statue of Lessing and Rachel Whiteread's Holocaust memorial, unveiled in 2000; the Constitutional Court sits here.
summaries.Q460607: This public aquarium occupies a concrete anti-aircraft tower 47 metres high, built during the Second World War, in Esterhazy Park in Mariahilf. It presents more than ten thousand aquatic creatures over about 4000 square metres. Since 1991 the building has carried a work by Lawrence Weiner, a memorial against war and fascism.
summaries.Q1491188: This neoclassical building in the Volksgarten was erected from 1819 to 1823 by Peter von Nobile in the Greek Revival style. A reduced-scale replica of the Temple of Theseus in Athens, it housed Antonio Canova's sculpture Theseus and the Centaur, moved to the Kunsthistorisches Museum in 1890. It now hosts temporary exhibitions.
summaries.Q59435: Opened in 2001, it grew out of the collection of Rudolf Leopold, who began buying then little-known artists in the 1950s and gathered 5,300 objects in all. It holds the world's largest collection of paintings by Egon Schiele, a large body of Austrian art and Gustav Klimt's Life and Death.
summaries.Q351228: Opened in 2000, it traces over 5,000 m2 the history of music and sound, from the first human uses of instruments to the present day, through interactive and multimedia displays. It occupies the palace of Archduke Charles, where Otto Nicolai, founder of the Vienna Philharmonic, lived, and won the Austrian Museum Prize in 2002.
summaries.Q664155: This Neo-Renaissance building was erected from 1861 to 1864 on the Kärntner Straße, facing the Opera, for the banker Baron Eduard von Todesco. Ludwig Foerster designed the architecture, Theophil von Hansen the interiors. Badly damaged during the Second World War and then restored, it was the seat of the Austrian People's Party from 1947 to 1993.
summaries.Q875751: Laid out in 1821 by Ludwig Remy on fortifications destroyed in 1809 by Napoleon's troops, this garden attached to the Hofburg was at first meant to stay private, reserved for the archdukes; it was opened to the public in 1823. It holds the Temple of Theseus, the monuments to Empress Elisabeth and to Franz Grillparzer, and over 3,000 rose bushes.
summaries.Q693869: Founded in 1327 by Duke Frederick the Fair together with its Augustinian monastery, it was the parish church of the Hofburg and thus of the Habsburgs. The nave was built between 1330 and 1339, but the consecration took place only in 1349. Several imperial weddings were celebrated there, including that of Marie Antoinette by proxy in 1770.
summaries.Q694757: Opened in 1876 in the former bank and exchange building now called Palais Ferstel, it became at the end of the 19th century one of the centres of Viennese intellectual life, frequented by Peter Altenberg, Theodor Herzl and Adolf Loos. Its many chess players earned it, until 1938, the nickname of the chess school.
summaries.Q167619: Founded in 1788, it is the oldest theatre in Vienna, one of the suburban theatres. After the building was completely rebuilt by Joseph Kornhäusel, Beethoven wrote and conducted Die Weihe des Hauses for the reopening in 1822. Camillo Castiglioni financed the 1923 renovation and handed the direction to Max Reinhardt.
summaries.Q874951: Lining the right bank of the Danube Canal, this square in the Innere Stadt is one of Vienna's main public transport hubs, served by the U1 and U4 metro lines and tram lines 1 and 2. From the Middle Ages until 1858 the Rotenturmtor, a gate in the city wall, stood there. The present name was given in 1919, in thanks for Swedish aid.
summaries.Q2167653: A former barracks in eclectic style built from 1865 to 1869 in the Rossau quarter of the 9th district, it first bore the name of Crown Prince Rudolf barracks and was raised, together with the Franz Joseph barracks and the Arsenal, to protect the city from the proletariat after the Revolution of 1848. It houses the Austrian Ministry of Defence.
summaries.Q1897966: A bronze copy of the stone column raised by Ferdinand III in memory of the city's deliverance from the Swedish army in 1645, it was commissioned in 1664 from the founder Balthasar Herold and erected in 1667 on Am Hof. Herold cast the pillar and the figures, designed by Lodovico Burnacini, from cannons taken from the enemy.
summaries.Q689951: A museum of modern and contemporary art opened in 1962 in the 20er Haus, it reopened in 2001 in the MuseumsQuartier, in a cube-shaped building of volcanic rock designed by Ortner & Ortner. Its collection brings together works by Picasso, Warhol, Beuys and Richter. The collectors Peter and Irene Ludwig gave it more than 230 works in 1981.
summaries.Q672373: Attached to the antiquities collection of the Kunsthistorisches Museum, it has occupied rooms in the Neue Burg, at the Hofburg, since December 1978. Its pieces come from the Austrian excavations at Ephesus, Sultan Abdülhamid II having given Franz Joseph part of the objects found. It shows the frieze of the Parthian Monument and the Apoxyomenos.
summaries.Q670935: Work on this Baroque palace began in 1717 under Johann Lucas von Hildebrandt, for Count Wirich Philipp von Daun; his son sold it in 1784 to the Kinsky princes, hence the name Palais Daun-Kinsky. General Joseph Poniatowski was born there in 1763. Restored in the late 1990s, it houses shops and a restaurant.
summaries.Q688588: Vienna's first public park, opened in 1862 to a design by the landscape gardener Joseph Selleny, it covers 95,931 m2 and is split in two by the river Wien. No Viennese park has as many sculptures: the western part, with wooded meadows, carries the gilded statue of Johann Strauss II; the eastern part has playgrounds and sports facilities.
summaries.Q688468: A Catholic church in the 1st district, also called Our Lady of the Snows, it succeeded the sanctuary founded on the site around 1224 by Franciscan Friars Minor. The present building, in French Gothic style, dates from 1339. Joseph II gave it to Vienna's Italian community. It holds a mosaic copy of Leonardo da Vinci's Last Supper.
summaries.Q254425: A pastry shop and chocolate maker founded in 1786 on Michaelerplatz by Ludwig Dehne, it passed in 1857 to Christof Demel, who moved the business to the Kohlmarkt, into the Palais Blankenstein, a Baroque building near the Hofburg. A former imperial and royal court supplier, it stayed with the Demels until 1972 and has belonged to Do & Co since 2002.
summaries.Q688555: This theatre in Vienna's 7th district (Neubau), formerly the Deutsches Volkstheater, was built to plans by Ferdinand Fellner and Hermann Helmer and opened in 1889. It stands at Neustiftgasse 1, opposite the Natural History Museum, near the Museumsquartier and Spittelberg. Kay Voges has directed it since 2020.
summaries.Q3573245: A square in the Innere Stadt bordered by the Redoutensaal, the library and the Augustinerkirche, it stands on the site of the Augustinian cemetery and has borne the name of Emperor Joseph II since 1786. At its centre is his equestrian statue by Franz Anton Zauner, unveiled in 1807. It served as an exterior location for The Third Man in 1948.
summaries.Q620532: Founded perhaps around 1440, and at the latest in 1568, the pharmacy changed address several times before settling on Bognergasse, in the Innere Stadt, in 1891. The building was demolished in 1901 for a Vienna Secession structure by Oskar Laske and Viktor Fiala. Two mosaic angels, designed by Laske, frame the shop window.
summaries.Q40300767: Erected in 1880 on Beethovenplatz, this bronze statue is the work of Caspar von Zumbusch, named winner of the competition in 1874. Beethoven is seated, surrounded by Prometheus, Victory and nine music-making putti, allegories of his 9 symphonies. The monument gives the square its name.
summaries.Q694810: Sigmund Freud moved in 1891 to 19 Berggasse, in the Alsergrund quarter: he practised there and founded psychoanalysis over 47 years, until he left for exile in London in 1938. Anna Freud opened her own practice there in 1923. In 1971 the apartment became a museum of the history of psychoanalysis, opened in the presence of Anna Freud.
summaries.Q83423523: The Albertina museum's second site, opened on 12 March 2020 in the Künstlerhaus on Karlsplatz, chosen in 2016 and fitted out over more than 2,000 m2. The holdings comprise 60,000 works by 5,000 artists: Hans Peter Haselsteiner had acquired 60% of the Essl collection, the remaining 40% of which was given to the Albertina.
summaries.Q692117: Raised on the foundations of Vienna's old city wall, this neoclassical palace designed in 1839 by Karl Schleps for Prince Ferdinand of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha was completed in 1845 by the builder Adolf Korompay. Occupied by Soviet troops until 1955 and renovated from 2000 to 2003, it houses a luxury hotel and two restaurants.
summaries.Q677602: Founded in 1754 by the faculty of natural sciences as a hortus medicus of medicinal plants, it adjoins the Belvedere gardens. Endlicher turned it into an English garden in 1841. Greenhouses, buildings and collections were destroyed by the bombing of the Second World War; part of it reopened in 1970. It holds 9,500 species.
summaries.Q688472: Built from 1623 to 1627 on the site of an earlier chapel, it was first dedicated to Saint Ignatius of Loyola and Saint Francis Xavier. Invited by Emperor Leopold I, the Jesuit brother Andrea Pozzo remodelled it in 1703-1705 and rebuilt the facade in Baroque style. The richly decorated interior has a large trompe-l'oeil dome.
summaries.Q1630919: Built in 1863 as the town palace of Duke Philipp of Württemberg, the building was sold in 1871 and turned into a hotel for the World's Fair of 1873. The yellow and white facade is in Italian Neo-Renaissance style. Samuel Schallinger, a pre-war co-owner, was forced to sell in 1938; he died in 1942 at Theresienstadt.
summaries.Q688568: Founded on 28 November 1893 in the 6th district, Mariahilf, it bears the name of the playwright Ferdinand Raimund. Adam Müller-Guttenbrunn ran it until 1896 and staged classical drama there, against the grain of bourgeois operettas. Rudolf Marik produced operettas there from 1948 to 1976, after which musicals have been staged intermittently.
summaries.Q457381: This square in the Innere Stadt runs between Am Hof and the Schottenstift, a monastery founded in 1158 by Irish monks. Its name probably comes from the exemption from municipal jurisdiction obtained by the monastery; it has applied to the whole square since 1710. Lined with palaces, it is best known for its markets.
summaries.Q2568865: Built on the Ringstrasse in a historicist style, it followed the plans of Theophil Hansen, accepted in 1869; the architect was raising the Parliament at the same time. The first stock exchange session was held there on 19 March 1877. Damaged by a bomb in 1945 and by a fire in 1956, its rooms are now rented out for events.
summaries.Q15850285: Raised at Praterstern in memory of Vice Admiral Wilhelm von Tegetthoff, it was unveiled on 21 September 1886 in the presence of Franz Joseph I. The 1872 competition had been won by Ferdinand Schlöth, but the commission went to Carl Kundmann, a member of the jury. A statue of nearly 3.5 metres crowns the 16-metre rostral column.
summaries.Q387667: The only surviving Mozart residence in Vienna, it housed him from 1784 to 1787. Built in the 17th century and enlarged in 1716, it is also known as the Camesina house, after the family that owned it from 1720. The original entrance, on the Schulerstraße, was walled up: the museum is entered from the Domgasse.
summaries.Q871525: A Celtic settlement that became a Roman camp, Vindobona stood on the site of present-day Vienna, in the province of Pannonia. According to Aurelius Victor, Marcus Aurelius set up his headquarters there during the Marcomannic wars and died there on 17 March 180. Its asymmetrical plan is still legible in the line of the Graben and the Salzgries.
summaries.Q610784: Built for Count Mollard from 1696 to 1698, this Baroque palace on the Herrengasse was bought in 1760 by Franz Wenzel von Clary-und-Aldringen, who made it his family's Viennese residence. Its courtyard holds a well topped by a wrought-iron grille of 1570. The National Library has housed the Globe Museum there since 2005.
summaries.Q2048203: A first neoclassical glasshouse was built in the Burggarten from 1823 to 1826; the present palm house, in Art Nouveau style, was designed by Friedrich Ohmann and raised between 1902 and 1906. Closed in 1988 for safety reasons and renovated from 1996 to 1998, it holds a restaurant, a butterfly house and a greenhouse.
summaries.Q701837: Vienna's oldest Marian shrine, it keeps the remains of Saint Clement Mary Hofbauer, patron of the city, and remains a place of pilgrimage. Deconsecrated in 1786, it served as an arsenal and a stable under the Napoleonic occupation of 1809, before being restored and reconsecrated in 1812, then entrusted to the Redemptorists.
summaries.Q264318: Opened on 1 October 1873 by Franz Landtmann, it is among the best known cafes in Vienna and stands on the west side of the Ring. The Querfeld family has owned it since 1976. Sigmund Freud, Gustav Mahler, Oskar Kokoschka, Romy Schneider and Marlene Dietrich all passed through.
summaries.Q1266829: A historicist building in Italian Renaissance style, it was erected in the Stadtpark between 1865 and 1867 by the architect Johann Garben on behalf of the city. Johann Strauss the younger gave his first concert there in October 1868, after which the place became a dance and concert hall. Hans Hübner leased it in 1908 and gave it his name.
summaries.Q451334: Within the Roman camp of Vindobona, this square was from 1155 to about 1275 the seat of the Babenbergs: Henry II of Austria had his residence built there after leaving Klosterneuburg. It held markets in 1340 and served as a place of execution. During the revolution of 1848 the crowd killed the war minister Baillet von Latour there.
summaries.Q877579: A ball-shaped house 8 m in diameter, built in 1971 by the artist Edwin Lipburger at Katzelsdorf without a building permit: a court case brought him ten weeks in prison. In 1976 he declared the independence of the Republic of Kugelmugel, which is not recognised. The ball moved to the Prater in June 1982.
summaries.Q2358079: A former gate in Vienna's city wall, known as the Hungarian Gate: the oldest dates from 1200, it was rebuilt after the Turkish siege of 1529, then in Renaissance style in 1555 and 1556, with a 25 m bell tower. Funeral processions passed through it towards St. Marx Cemetery; Mozart's cortege stopped there. The wall was demolished in 1862.
summaries.Q1824069: Housed in the Palais Liechtenstein, a Baroque building in Alsergrund, it brings together the collections of the Princes of Liechtenstein, one of the world's largest private art collections: nearly 1,600 paintings from the Renaissance to the Biedermeier. Opened in 2004 and closed in 2011 for lack of visitors, it now takes only groups by booking.
summaries.Q211818: One of the largest Baroque palaces in Vienna, built from 1714 to 1723 by Johann Lukas von Hildebrandt for Prince Eugene of Savoy: the Upper Belvedere overlooks the gardens, the Lower Belvedere faces it. It has housed a museum since 1903, with the Gustav Klimt collection. The State Treaty was signed there on 15 May 1955.
summaries.Q471908: One of the most important Baroque buildings in Vienna, it was built in 1712 for Count Trautson to plans by Johann Bernhard Fischer von Erlach, with a richly decorated three-storey facade. Maria Theresa bought it in 1760 and made it available to the Hungarian royal guard. The Ministry of Justice sits there.
summaries.Q1014945: A pleasure garden, it lies on a former glacis at the foot of Vienna's city wall, of which a single bastion stood after the destruction of the city by the French in 1809. At first the emperor's private garden, it took the form of an English park, then extended towards the Ring in 1863. Opened to the public in 1919, it holds a palm house.
summaries.Q695388: Raised from 1698 to 1719, probably to plans by Lukas von Hildebrandt for the Piarist order, it owes its name to a grace image painted during the plague epidemic of 1713. Its convex facade is the only Viennese example of its kind. Franz Anton Maulbertsch, a late Baroque painter, made five frescoes there.
summaries.Q1536160: Opened in 1870 on the Ring, it was Vienna's first luxury hotel, with more than 300 rooms, a steam lift and a telegraph office, to plans by Carl Tietz. It housed Soviet troops from 1945 to 1955, reopened in 1958, then was leased to the IAEA, which had its seat there until 1979. Bought back and renovated, it reopened in 1994.
summaries.Q267329: Vienna's first district is the old town: until the annexations of the 1850s it made up the entire city. Its four quarters are named after former gates, and the Ringstrasse has marked its edge since the walls came down. It counts more than 60 museums and has the smallest population in Vienna.
summaries.Q337357: A monumental stairway in Alsergrund, it is built of Mannersdorf limestone to plans by Theodor Johann Jaeger and was opened on 29 November 1910. Symmetrical in its lower part, which includes two fountains, it has two curved flights. Some parts, green today, were originally blue. A novel of 1951 made it famous.
summaries.Q688614: Standing on the Graben, it arose from a vow by Leopold I: the emperor, who had fled Vienna during the plague epidemic of 1679, promised a column if the scourge ceased. A temporary wooden column preceded the final monument, which passed through the hands of several sculptors and was unveiled in 1694. It marks Vienna's turn towards the Baroque.
summaries.Q33701: Set in St. Stephen's Cathedral, this monumental tomb was planned as early as 1463 by Frederick III, who brought in the sculptor Nicolaus of Leyden; he finished only the top slab before dying in 1473. Max Valmet and then Michael Tichter took over the work, completed in 1513: the emperor, who died in 1493, never saw his tomb finished.
summaries.Q317701: Housed in the Swiss Wing of the Hofburg, it lays out in 21 rooms the objects the Habsburgs held to carry the greatest dynastic or religious meaning: on one side the regalia of the Holy Roman Empire and the Austrian jewels, on the other relics and objects attributed to saints. It comes under the Kunsthistorisches Museum.
summaries.Q686468: Seat of the city council and of the Vienna Landtag, the building was designed by Friedrich von Schmidt in a Neo-Gothic style inspired by the town hall of Brussels and built from 1872 to 1883. The Rathausmann, atop the main tower, reaches 97.9 metres. The central balcony was built for Adolf Hitler, who gave a speech there on 9 April 1938.
summaries.Q459952: Raised in 1783-1784 for Count Johann von Fries on the Josefsplatz, opposite the Hofburg, it was the first Viennese palace with a neoclassical facade. Contemporaries found it too plain: in 1786 Fries commissioned caryatids from Franz Anton von Zauner. The Pallavicini bought it in 1842. The Third Man made it Harry Lime's house.
summaries.Q1117261: The oldest surviving Jewish cemetery in Austria: Vienna's Jewish community buried its dead there from 1540 to 1783, before the sanitary rules of Joseph II closed it. All the inscriptions on the stones are in Hebrew. The ground, about 2,000 m2, forms part of the courtyard of a retirement home. Access is closed for works.
summaries.Q689008: Of Vienna's surviving churches, this is the one with the oldest foundations. Built within the area of the former Roman camp of Vindobona, it remained the only parish until that role passed to St. Stephen's in 1147. Its oldest walls date from the early 12th century; the apse keeps the oldest stained glass in the city.
summaries.Q37865047: Opened on 26 June 1892 as the Hotel am Ring, it stands on the Ringstrasse near the Opera and has 127 rooms and 23 suites; Art Deco marks its public areas, all of them protected. Samuel Schallinger was expropriated by the Nazis in 1938 under Aryanisation, then killed at Theresienstadt in 1942. No restitution followed.
summaries.Q46232: A ring boulevard laid out on the site of the ramparts, it encircles the centre and bounds the first district. On 20 December 1857 Franz Joseph signed the decree instructing his minister to prepare the enlargement of the capital: the walls were dismantled and the boulevard lined with public buildings, palaces and tenement houses.
summaries.Q390534: This Art Nouveau stairway in Mariahilf, built from 1905 to 1907 to a design by Max Hegele, links the Fillgradergasse to the Theobaldgasse. Closed in 1981 and repaired between 1982 and 1984, it reopened on 1 August 1985 with a cafe and a gallery. A 2004 survey of European art professors ranked it the fourth most beautiful stairway in Europe.
summaries.Q697578: Built in 1896-1897 to plans by the English architects Walter Basset and Harry Hitchens, it stands at the entrance to the Prater, in Leopoldstadt. It was the tallest Ferris wheel in the world between 1920 and 1985. Burnt out in a bombing raid in 1944, it was rebuilt in 1953 with only 15 of its original 30 cabins.
summaries.Q46242: Vienna's largest palace was built in stages from the 13th century, around a core raised about 1220 under the Babenbergs. A Habsburg residence for more than 600 years, it has over 2,600 rooms spread across 18 wings and holds the imperial apartments; since 1946 it has been the state residence of the federal president.
summaries.Q549585: A Benedictine abbey founded in 1155, when Henry II Jasomirgott called to Vienna monks known as Irish-Scottish, who came from St. James's Abbey near Regensburg and not directly from the British Isles. Albert V took it from the Scots in 1418 to hand it to the Benedictines, but the name stuck. Its museum keeps a late Gothic altar.
summaries.Q702121: Seat of the National Council and the Federal Council, this neoclassical building was raised on the Ringstrasse from 1874 to 1883 for the sessions of the Imperial Council. Theophil Hansen drew on Greek architecture, familiar to him from a long stay in Athens. Half the building was destroyed in the fighting of 1945 and rebuilt in June 1956.
summaries.Q877068: Raised for the Austrian National Bank to plans by Heinrich von Ferstel, it was to bring together the bank, the stock exchange, a cafe and a bazaar; bank and exchange were completed there in 1860. The exchange left in 1872, the bank in 1925. Renovated from 1975 to 1982, it has since been known as Palais Ferstel, where Cafe Central has reopened.
summaries.Q5943: Gothic in the middle of a Baroque quarter, it was begun in 1137 and consecrated in 1147 while still under construction; it has been a cathedral only since 1469. Its south tower reaches 136.4 m, the north tower was left unfinished. Its glazed tile roof carries, on the east side, the double-headed eagle of Austria-Hungary.
summaries.Q688524: Dedicated to Saint Jerome, it is the church of the Franciscan order in Vienna, with a Renaissance facade and a Baroque interior. In 1589 the Franciscans were given the use of a monastery built between 1383 and 1387, until then held by the Penitents; the church was built in 1607 and its interior completed around 1720.
summaries.Q209937: The first of the great Ring projects, the building was erected from 1861 to 1869 by August Sicard von Sicardsburg and Eduard van der Nüll, in a Neo-Renaissance style that drew fierce criticism; neither of them saw it completed. Gutted by fire in a bombing raid in 1945, it reopened on 5 November 1955 with Fidelio.
summaries.Q700128: Laid out in front of the Hofburg on the site of the bastion blown up by Napoleon's troops in 1809, it was arranged under Franz Joseph as part of the Kaiserforum, a project begun in 1871 and never completed. Named in 1878 after the heroes of its two equestrian statues, it saw Hitler proclaim the Anschluss in 1938.
summaries.Q783523: On the Freyung, a white stone column carries a victorious Austria, the personification of the country, lance and shield in hand. Four allegories surround her, those of the most important rivers of the Habsburg empire: the Elbe, the Danube, the Vistula and the Po. The fountain was designed in 1844 by Ludwig Schwanthaler.
summaries.Q177008: Planned from February 1945 by the Soviet command and built just after the war, the monument sets out a semicircular colonnade of white marble 8 metres high with 26 columns, partly enclosing a Red Army soldier twelve metres tall. It is dedicated to the 17,000 Soviet soldiers killed in the Vienna offensive.
summaries.Q95569: Opened in 1891 on the Ring, in an Italian Renaissance building designed from the outset for the purpose, the museum holds the collections gathered over the centuries by the House of Habsburg: Egyptian and Greco-Roman antiquities, the Kunstkammer, the coin cabinet, paintings. Its twin, the Natural History Museum, stands opposite.
summaries.Q689043: Completed in 1700 for Prince Johann Adam I of Liechtenstein, to plans by Domenico Egidio Rossi and then Domenico Martinelli, this Baroque palace in the Rossau quarter still belongs to the princely family. It showed its collections there in a museum open to the public from 1805 to 1938. The Liechtenstein Museum opened in 2004.
summaries.Q651030: Begun in 1697 by Lukas von Hildebrandt, this Baroque palace of the princely Schwarzenberg family was finished in 1728 under Johann Bernhard Fischer von Erlach, with Anton Erhard Martinelli supervising the work. A riding hall and an orangery were added in 1751. Part of it now serves as a five-star hotel.
summaries.Q873416: Designed by Andreas Streit and built in 1887-91 for the American company The Equitable Life Assurance Society, the building is one of the few Viennese palaces never to have been an aristocratic residence. Its richly decorated facade features American eagles. It now houses offices of companies and organisations.
summaries.Q408847: This votive church arose from a vow by Emperor Charles VI during the Vienna plague of 1713 and honours his patron saint, Charles Borromeo. Johann Bernhard Fischer von Erlach drew the plans and followed the work until his death in 1723; his son Joseph Emanuel completed it in 1737. Two carved columns frame the entrance portico.
summaries.Q877807: In the historic Greek quarter of the Innere Stadt, known as Fleischmarkt, this Orthodox cathedral is a Neo-Byzantine redesign by Theophil Hansen of the building raised in 1787 by Peter Mollner. The diplomat Simon Sina financed the project. Opened in 1858, it has been the seat of the Greek Orthodox Metropolis of Austria since 1963.
summaries.Q308720: Founded in 1741 under Maria Theresa as a court theatre, it is the second oldest theatre in Europe after the Comedie-Francaise, and the largest in the German language. The present building, Neo-Renaissance and Neo-Baroque, designed by Karl von Hasenauer and Gottfried Semper, opened in 1888 on the Ring and seats 1,285.
summaries.Q700753: This square lies on the boundary between the Innere Stadt and Wieden districts. Dominated by the Karlskirche, it is among the busiest in the city.
summaries.Q1558800: The work of Anton Paul Wagner, this fountain shows a young girl with a goose, a motif chosen for its original setting: the poultry market on the Brandstätte, where it stood from 1866. Removed in 1874, then set up in front of the Mariahilf church from 1879, it reached the top of the Rahlstiege stairway in 1886.
summaries.Q869983: This reinforced concrete block on the Judenplatz, the work of the British sculptor Rachel Whiteread and unveiled in 2000, is dedicated to the 65,000 Austrian Jews murdered by the Nazis between 1938 and 1945. It shows shelves of books with their spines turned inwards, hence its other name, the Nameless Library.
summaries.Q371908: Fitted out in 1801 to hold the drawings, prints and watercolours gathered by Duke Albert of Saxe-Teschen, son-in-law of Maria Theresa, the palace is now a museum. Its graphic arts collection is among the richest in the world, and its 139 drawings and watercolours by Dürer form the largest such group anywhere.
summaries.Q686488: Housed in the Hofburg, this ethnographic museum, opened in 1928 as the Museum für Völkerkunde, was renamed Weltmuseum Wien in 2013, then reopened after works on 25 October 2017. Its collections include the collection of the navigator James Cook and bronzes from the Kingdom of Benin.
summaries.Q877570: Built by the architect Otto Wagner, the Postal Savings Bank (Postsparkasse) is an Art Nouveau building characteristic of the Vienna Secession. It stands at number 2 Georg Coch-Platz, in the eastern quadrant of the city centre.
summaries.Q876884: A Neo-Renaissance building raised between 1875 and 1881 to plans by Alexander Wielemans von Monteforte, it houses the Supreme Court of Austria. Burnt in 1927 during the July Revolt, it was rebuilt in the early 1930s and gained a storey. Its entrance hall, 23 metres high, is topped by a glass dome.
summaries.Q662652: In 1618 Empress Anna asked by will for a tomb for herself and her husband at the Capuchin friary. Building began in 1622 and it was in 1633 that Emperor Matthias and his wife were buried there. Enlarged eight times, the crypt gathers one hundred and forty-nine people, among them twelve emperors and nineteen empresses and queens.
summaries.Q700863: A Catholic church dedicated to Saint John the Baptist, on the Kärntner Straße, it belonged to the Order of Saint John of Jerusalem. Mentioned as early as 1217 as a hospitaller commandery for crusaders, it occupies a building of the mid-15th century, rebuilt in 1806. The Sovereign Order of Malta, in financial difficulty, sold it in 1933.
summaries.Q686720: Opened on 6 January 1870, this concert hall built by the architect Theophil Hansen on land given by Emperor Franz Joseph owes its reputation to the acoustics of its Golden Hall, which has 1,744 seats. It is the home of the Vienna Philharmonic Orchestra and hosts the New Year's Concert each year.
summaries.Q701662: Vienna's central square and the zero point from which distances to the country's national borders are measured, it is occupied in its middle by St. Stephen's Cathedral, work on which began in 1137. It took shape from the 17th century, when the buildings adjoining the cathedral were demolished.
summaries.Q1240976: Opened in October 1861 in the bazaar courtyard of the Palais Ferstel, between Freyung and Herrengasse, it was designed by Heinrich von Ferstel. Three bronze mermaids dance around the column that rises from the marble basin and is crowned by an allegory of the Danube holding a small fish. The whole reaches 6 metres in height.
summaries.Q18346455: A Lasa marble statue represents the musician Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart. Made in 1896 by the architect Karl König and the sculptor Viktor Tilgner, the monument was unveiled on 8 April of the same year. First placed on the Albertinaplatz, it has stood in the Burggarten since 1953.
summaries.Q304037: Founded in the late Middle Ages by the Austrian dukes of the House of Habsburg, it bore the name of Court Library until 1920. Housed in the Hofburg, it holds more than 12 million items, including nearly 4 million books, which makes it the richest library in Austria. Its State Hall is 80 metres long.
summaries.Q284902: Built from 1865 to 1868 by August Weber in the Ringstrasse area, in a style drawn from Italian Renaissance villas, the building has served since as an exhibition house and a venue for performances. In 1897 twenty artists, among them Gustav Klimt, left the Künstlerhaus cooperative to found the Vienna Secession.
summaries.Q873332: Built at the end of the 17th century by Johann Bernhard Fischer von Erlach for the alderman Zacharias Leeb, the palace became the property of Joseph II in 1780, then stayed with the Habsburg-Lorraines until the early 20th century. Heavily damaged during the Second World War and then restored, it was given in 1948 to the Vienna Boys' Choir.
summaries.Q774259: Raised between 1558 and 1565 as a residence for Emperor Maximilian II, this Renaissance building with an inner courtyard is part of the Hofburg. From 1659 to 1776, eleven rooms on the second floor held the art collection of Archduke Leopold Wilhelm. The building then served as the imperial stables; the Spanish Riding School still uses it.
summaries.Q254476: After the failed attempt on the life of Franz Joseph I by Libenyi in 1853, Archduke Ferdinand Maximilian launched a collection to which more than 300,000 citizens responded. The competition was won by Heinrich Ferstel, aged 26. Opened in 1879, the Neo-Gothic church has towers 99 metres high.
summaries.Q697944: Built in 1617 for the Capuchin fathers and consecrated in 1632, the church of Saint Mary of the Angels faces the Neuer Markt, near the Hofburg. Emperor Ferdinand II made it the burial place of the Habsburgs and was himself buried there in 1637: the crypt holds nearly one hundred and fifty family tombs.
summaries.Q374336: Commissioned by the impresario Emanuel Schikaneder, the theatre was built from 1798 to plans by Franz Jäger and opened on 13 June 1801. Its name comes not from the city but from the river Wien, on whose banks it was built. Beethoven premiered Fidelio and several of his symphonies there.
summaries.Q699937: The name means ditch: a ditch surrounded the Roman camp of Vindobona, then the walls of the castle in the Middle Ages. It disappeared at the end of the 12th century, when the Babenbergs enlarged the city with the ransom of Richard the Lionheart, and gave way to a street. The Graben remains one of Vienna's great shopping streets.
summaries.Q2517129: The sculptural group shows the marriage of Mary and Joseph. A first votive monument in wood, by Johann Bernhard Fischer von Erlach and going back to a vow by Leopold I, was erected on the Hoher Markt in 1706; worn out, it was pulled down in 1725. The present Baroque group, 18 metres high, was consecrated in 1732.
summaries.Q21234884: Standing since 1888 on Maria-Theresien-Platz, between the two former court museums, it commemorates the sovereign who led the Habsburg monarchy from 1740 to 1780. Franz Joseph I chose the design by Caspar Zumbusch, whose bronzes weigh 44 tonnes in all. The whole reaches 19.36 m in height.
summaries.Q265129: The work of Joseph Maria Olbrich, built in 1897, the building was an architectural manifesto and an exhibition hall for the Vienna Secession, a group of artists breaking with the older conception of the arts. It holds Klimt's Beethoven Frieze and carries above the entrance the motto "To every age its art, to every art its freedom".
summaries.Q874905: The winter palace of Prince Eugene of Savoy, it was built from 1697 to 1716 to plans by Fischer von Erlach, with Lukas von Hildebrandt working on it from 1702 to 1724. The building now houses the Austrian Ministry of Finance.
summaries.Q697572: Facing St. Stephen's Cathedral, this building by the architect Hans Hollein was opened in 1990. It replaces a post-war building which had itself succeeded the carpet shop "Philipp Haas und Söhne", whose name it took over. Its avant-garde architecture, so close to the old centre, remains contentious.
summaries.Q1674603: Part of the Hofburg and of the Kaiserforum that Gottfried Semper and Carl von Hasenauer designed from 1869, this neoclassical wing was authorised by Franz Joseph I in 1881. Its foundations go down 25 metres, the site resting on former moats. Work stopped in 1923 without being finished.
summaries.Q253663: Vienna's main synagogue, it was opened in 1826 to plans by Joseph Kornhäusel. Since non-Catholic worship then had to remain invisible from the street, the hall sits behind the facade of an apartment building. The only one of more than 90 synagogues spared by the flames in 1938, it was ransacked; Jews were held there and then deported.
summaries.Q251468: A Baroque pilgrimage church, it grew out of a wooden cemetery chapel built by the Barnabites in 1656, where the painting of Mary Help of Christians was placed. The stone chapel that followed was destroyed during the Turkish siege of Vienna, the painting having been put in safety. The present building dates from 1686 to 1689.
summaries.Q694747: Vienna's second opera stage after the state opera, the Volksoper occupies a building erected in 1898. It was at first given over entirely to drama, before operas and operettas were added to the programme from 1903.
summaries.Q417645: With 2.315 hectares between the two Wienzeile, from the Getreidemarkt to the Kettenbrückengasse station, it is the largest market in central Vienna. The farmers' market that appeared in 1780 on the right bank of the Wien was moved to this site only from 1902; the name Naschmarkt, recorded around 1820, became official in 1905.
summaries.Q18629666: Designed in 1870 by Theophil Hansen as part of the Parliament, it was begun only in 1898 and unveiled in 1902. An allegory of Austria was first planned as the main figure, before Pallas Athena was preferred, judged more neutral for the multi-ethnic monarchy. Standing 5.5 metres tall, the goddess turns her back on the Parliament.
summaries.Q1255665: The sculptor Alfred Hrdlicka made this memorial to the victims of Nazism and of the Second World War, installed in 1988 on the Albertinaplatz, behind the state opera. The site is that of the Philipphof, a building where hundreds of people died in a bombing raid on 12 March 1945; only 180 bodies were recovered.
summaries.Q699943: This cultural complex occupies the former imperial stables in the 7th district and was built between 1998 and 2001, joining the Baroque of the stables to modern buildings such as the Leopold Museum and the Mumok. It also brings together the Kunsthalle, the Architekturzentrum, the ZOOM children's museum and the Tanzquartier.
summaries.Q505873: This group brings together the museums devoted to the history of the city. Besides the main building on Karlsplatz and the Hermesvilla, it includes many specialised museums, musicians' residences and archaeological sites.
summaries.Q694760: Adolf Loos built it between 1909 and 1911 opposite the Hofburg, for the men's ready-to-wear shop Goldman & Salatsch: retail on the lower floors, apartments above. The ground floor is faced with marble, the upper part left without ornament. The absence of window canopies earned it the nickname of the house without eyebrows.
summaries.Q2047001: Aloys Thomas Raimund von Harrach had it raised on the Ungargasse by Lukas von Hildebrandt between 1727 and 1735, with two courtyards of honour and a chapel dedicated to Saint Januarius. Sold in 1791 to Leopold II, it was badly damaged by a bombing raid at the end of the Second World War; its ruins were cleared in 1968, except the chapel.
summaries.Q700199: Built from 1219 to 1221 at the request of Duke Leopold VI, it is a rare Viennese building in Romanesque style and one of the city's three parishes along with St. Stephen's and the Schottenstift. The Salvatorians have served it since 1923. The film Sissi shot the imperial wedding there, which in fact took place in the Augustinerkirche.
summaries.Q666683: The Dominicans settled in the Innere Stadt in 1226; their Romanesque chapel gave way in 1283 to a Gothic church, largely demolished during the Turkish siege of 1529. Ferdinand II commissioned a new Baroque one, consecrated in 1634; dome and facade followed from 1666 to 1674. It was then Vienna's largest church after St. Stephen's.
summaries.Q259553: This public educational institute, coupled with an astronomical observatory, was built in Art Nouveau style by Max Fabiani on the bank of the river Wien and opened in 1910 by Franz Joseph I. Badly damaged during the Second World War, it reopened in 1957 and holds seminar rooms and a theatre and cinema hall.
summaries.Q699952: Laid out on the Ring opposite the Hofburg, where the glacis stretched until 1857, it is framed by the two former court museums, the Kunsthistorisches Museum and the Natural History Museum. The monument to Maria Theresa, unveiled in 1888 and the largest Habsburg monument in Vienna, stands at its centre.
summaries.Q1689154: Set against the palace of Archduke Albert, this fountain was unveiled on 24 December 1869 to plans by Moritz von Loehr, with allegories by Johann Meixner representing Vindobona, the Danube and its tributaries. The bombing of 12 March 1945 left standing only Vindobona, Danubius, the Sava and the Tisza.
